# Today's Learning Goals

## By the end of this lecture, we will be able to...

-   Identify probability as a proportion that converges to the truth as you collect more data.
-   Calculate probabilities using the Inclusion-Exclusion Principle, the Law of Total Probability, and probability distributions.
-   Convert between and interpret odds and probability.

## And...

-   Specify the usefulness of odds over probability.
-   Be aware that probability has multiple interpretations/philosophies.
-   Calculate and interpret mean, mode, entropy, variance, and standard deviation, mainly from a distribution.

# Outline

1.  Thinking About of Probability
2.  Probability Distributions
3.  Measures of Central Tendency and Uncertainty

## 1. Thinking About of Probability

- <span style="color: purple;">Probability</span> is recurring throughout different Data Science-related topics.
- In MDS, you will find it in either the Statistics or Machine Learning courses.

![Mexican Lotería (photo by <a href="https://unsplash.com/@irvinmac?utm_source=unsplash&utm_medium=referral&utm_content=creditCopyText">irvin Macfarland</a> on <a href="https://unsplash.com/photos/clelay10tfg?utm_source=unsplash&utm_medium=referral&utm_content=creditCopyText">Unsplash</a>).](images/loteria.jpg){width="400" height="250"}

### 1.1. Defining Probability

<br>

Let $A$ be an event of interest, its probability is denoted as 
$$P(A) = \frac{\text{Number of times event $A$ is observed}}{\text{Total number of events observed}}$$

**as the *total number of events observed* goes to infinity**.

#### The Coin Toss

::: incremental
- Frequentist Statistics is the mainstream approach we learn in introductory courses.
- Let us illustrate the frequentist paradigm idea with the typical coin toss example.

![](images/coin_toss.png){fig-align="center" width=30%}

:::

#### System Insights

The coin toss represents our <span style="color: purple;">system</span> for which we assume two possible <span style="color: purple;">random outcomes</span>:

\begin{gather*}
H = \{ \text{Getting heads} \} \\
T = \{ \text{Getting tails} \}.
\end{gather*}

. . .

Our system has the following <span style="color: purple;">parameters of interest</span>:

\begin{gather*}
P(H) = \text{Probability of getting heads} \\
P(T) = \text{Probability of getting tails}.
\end{gather*}

#### Probabilistic Inquiries

<br>

Suppose this coin is unfair, i.e.,
$$P(H) \neq P(T) \neq \frac{1}{2};$$

. . .

and we want to <span style="color: purple;">estimate</span> these two <span style="color: purple;">unknown</span> probabilities!

#### Now, think about the following questions:

<br>

::: incremental
a. How would you <span style="color: purple;">estimate</span> these two <span style="color: purple;">unknown probabilities</span>?
b. What are the characteristics of these two <span style="color: purple;">estimated probabilities</span>?

![](images/coin_toss.png){fig-align="center" width=30%}
:::

#### Answers

<br>

::: incremental
a. Tossing the coin a given number of times $n$ and obtaining the proportions for both $H$ and $T$.
b. Ideally, they will more <span style="color: purple;">accurate</span> and <span style="color: purple;">precise</span> as $n$ tends to infinity.

![](images/coin_toss.png){fig-align="center" width=30%}
:::

### 1.2. Calculating Probabilities using Laws

<br>

::: incremental
- Let us start with two fundamental laws that will allow us to exercise our probabilistic reasoning:
  * **Law of Total Probability**.
  * **Inclusion-Exclusion Principle**.
:::

#### Sample Space ($S$)

. . .

- It is the collection of all the possible outcomes of a <span style="color: purple;">random process or system</span>. 

. . .


- <span style="color: purple;">Each one of these outcomes has a probability associated with it.</span>
- Note that 
$$P(S) = 1.$$

#### Law of Total Probability

::: incremental
- Breaks down the sample space $S$ of a random process or system into disjoint parts.
- We can obtain specific probabilities based on <span style="color: purple;">sample space partitions</span>.

![](images/jigsaw-puzzle.jpg){fig-align="center" width=40%}
:::

#### The Mario Kart Example

:::{style="font-size: 30px;"}
|Item | Name | Probability| Combat Type  | Defeats Blue Shells |
|:---:|:-------:|:----------:|:------:|:---------:|
| ![](images/banana.png){height="40"} | Banana  |     0.12| contact | no |
| ![](images/bobomb.png){height="40"} | Bob-omb |     0.05| explosion  | no |
| ![](images/coin.png){height="40"}   | Coin    |     0.75| ineffective | no |
| ![](images/horn.png){height="40"}   | Horn    |     0.03| explosion | yes |
| ![](images/shell.png){height="40"}  | Shell   |     0.05| contact | no |

> **Attribution:** Images from [pngkey](https://www.pngkey.com/detail/u2w7e6o0i1q8i1y3_randome-clipart-mario-kart-mario-kart-8-deluxe/).
:::

#### Now, think about the following questions:

. . .

1. Are there any other items possible? Why or why not?
2. What is the probability of getting something other than a coin?

![](images/panda.png){fig-align="center" width=30%}

#### Answers

. . .

1. We use the concept of the sample space:

$$1 = P(\text{Banana}) + P(\text{Bob-omb}) + P(\text{Coin}) + P(\text{Horn}) + P(\text{Shell}).$$
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.5
library(treemapify)
library(tidyverse)

item_box_prob <- tibble(
  item = c("Banana", "Bob-omb", "Coin", "Horn", "Shell"),
  defeat = c(rep("no", 3), "yes", "no"),
  prob = c(0.12, 0.05, 0.75, 0.03, 0.05)
)

ggplot(item_box_prob, aes(
  area = prob, fill = item,
  label = paste(item, prob, sep = "\n")
)) +
  geom_treemap() +
  geom_treemap_text(
    colour = "white",
    place = "centre",
    size = 14
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),
  ) +
  ggtitle("Partition of the Sample Space S for the Outcome of the Item Box")
```

#### And...

. . .

2. We use another probability concept called the <span style="color: purple;">complement</span> of an event (check the below  <span style="color: purple;">Venn diagram</span>):
$$P(\text{Coin}^c) = 1 - P(\text{Coin}) = 1 - 0.75 = 0.25.$$

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11.5
#| fig-height: 3

library(eulerr)
coin_venn <- euler(c("Coin" = 0.75))

plot(coin_venn,
  quantities = list(fontsize = 16), fills = "lightskyblue",
  labels = list(cex = 1.2),
  main = "\n Sample Space S of an Item Box"
)
```

#### Inclusion and Exclusion Principle

. . .

- Let $A$ and $B$ be two events of interest in the sample space $S$:
$$P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B).$$
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11.5
#| fig-height: 3.5

AB_venn <- euler(c("A" = 0.75, "B" = 0.75, "A&B" = 0.1))

plot(AB_venn,
  quantities = FALSE,
  fills = c("rosybrown1", "lightsteelblue1"),
  labels = list(cex = 1.2),
  main = "\n Sample Space S"
)
```

#### Extension to Three Events

. . .

- Let $A$, $B$, and $C$ be three events of interest in the sample space $S$:
\begin{align*}
P(A \cup B \cup C) &= P(A) + P(B) + P(C) - P(A \cap B) - P(B \cap C) \\
& \qquad - P(A \cap C) + P(A \cap B \cap C)
\end{align*}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 2.7

ABC_venn <- euler(c(
  "A" = 0.75, "B" = 0.75, "C" = 0.75,
  "A&B" = 0.1, "A&C" = 0.1, "B&C" = 0.1,
  "A&B&C" = 0.1
))

plot(ABC_venn,
  quantities = FALSE, 
  fills = c("rosybrown1", "lightsteelblue1", "moccasin"),
  labels = list(cex = 1.2),
  main = "\n Sample Space S"
)
```

#### Now, let us answer the following questions:

. . .

3. Using the below table, what is the probability of getting an item with an explosion combat type (event $E$)?

:::{style="font-size: 17px;"}
|Item | Name | Probability| Combat Type  | Defeats Blue Shells |
|:---:|:-------:|:----------:|:------:|:---------:|
| ![](images/banana.png){height="40"} | Banana  |     0.12| contact | no |
| ![](images/bobomb.png){height="40"} | Bob-omb |     0.05| explosion  | no |
| ![](images/coin.png){height="40"}   | Coin    |     0.75| ineffective | no |
| ![](images/horn.png){height="40"}   | Horn    |     0.03| explosion | yes |
| ![](images/shell.png){height="40"}  | Shell   |     0.05| contact | no |

> **Attribution:** Images from [pngkey](https://www.pngkey.com/detail/u2w7e6o0i1q8i1y3_randome-clipart-mario-kart-mario-kart-8-deluxe/).
:::

#### Mutually Exclusive (or Disjoint) Events

. . .

- Two events are mutually exclusive (or disjoint) <span style="color: purple;">if they cannot happen at the same time</span> in the sample space $S$:

$$
P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - \underbrace{P(A \cap B)}_{0} = P(A) + P(B).
$$

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 2.5

ABC_venn <- euler(c(
  "A" = 0.75, "B" = 0.75
))

plot(ABC_venn,
  quantities = FALSE, 
  fills = c("rosybrown1", "lightsteelblue1"),
  labels = list(cex = 1.2),
  main = "\n Sample Space S"
)
```

#### Answer

. . .

We can compute this probability by adding up the following probabilities:

$$P(E) = P(\text{Bob-omb}) + P(\text{Horn}) = 0.05 + 0.03 = 0.08.$$

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11.5
#| fig-height: 3

q3_venn <- euler(c("Bob-omb" = 0.05, "Horn" = 0.03))

plot(q3_venn,
  quantities = list(fontsize = 16), fills = c(
    "thistle1",
    "lightyellow"
  ),
  labels = list(cex = 1.5),
  main = "\n Sample Space S of an Item Box"
)
```

#### Then...

. . .

4. What is the probability of getting an item that is both an explosion item (event $E$) and defeats blue shells (event $D$)?

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11.5
#| fig-height: 4.5

q4_venn <- euler(c("E" = 0.08, "E&D" = 0.03))

plot(q4_venn,
  quantities = list(fontsize = 16), fills = c("lightskyblue", "khaki1"),
  labels = list(cex = 1.5),
  main = "\n Sample Space S of an Item Box "
)
```

#### Answer

<br>

. . .

This probability can be obtained as

$$P(E \cap D) = P(\text{Horn}) = 0.03.$$

This intersection is actually equal to the probability of getting a Horn.

#### Finally...

. . .

5. What is the probability of getting an item that is an explosion item (event $E$) or an item that defeats blue shells (event $D$)?

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11.5
#| fig-height: 4.2

plot(q4_venn,
  quantities = list(fontsize = 16), fills = c("lightskyblue", "khaki1"),
  labels = list(cex = 1.5),
  main = "\n Sample Space S of an Item Box "
)
```

#### Answer

<br>

. . .

By the Inclusion-Exclusion Principle, we have that

\begin{align*}
P(E \cup D) &= P(E) + P(D) - P(E \cap D) \\
&= 0.08 + 0.03 - 0.03 \\
&= 0.08.
\end{align*}

#### Independent Events

<br>

::: incremental
- Two events are independent <span style="color: purple;">if the occurrence of one of them does not affect the probability of the other</span>. 
- Their intersection is defined as:
$$P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B).$$
:::

### 1.3. Comparing Probabilities

<br>

::: incremental
- We might be interested in <span style="color: purple;">comparing two probabilities</span>.
- Suppose an event has a probability $p$ of happening. 
:::

#### The Odds

::: incremental
- The <span style="color: purple;">odds</span> $o$ are defined as the ratio of this probability to the probability of not happening $1 - p$:
$$o = \frac{p}{1 - p}.$$
- With some algebraic rearrangements, we can obtain $p$ with the odds:
$$p = \frac{o}{o+1}.$$
:::

#### Example

::: incremental
- If you win 80% of the times at solitaire, i.e., $p = 0.8$; then your odds are:
$$o = \frac{p}{1 - p} = \frac{0.8}{0.2} = 4$$
- This is sometimes written as 4:1 odds -- that is, *four wins for every loss*.

![](images/cards.png){fig-align="center" width=10%}
:::

## 2. Probability Distributions

<br>

::: incremental
- A <span style="color: purple;">probability distribution</span> is the set of all outcomes and their corresponding probabilities. 
- The outcome itself, which is uncertain, is called a <span style="color: purple;">random variable</span>; e.g.,
$$X = \text{Number of customers standing in line at a bank branch.}$$
:::

### Types of Random Variables

<br>

In general, random variables are classified as:

<br>

::: incremental
- <span style="color: purple;">Continuous:</span> it can take on a set of uncountable outcomes.
- <span style="color: purple;">Discrete:</span> it can take on a set of countable outcomes.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-left}
> **Heads-up:** A continuous random variable has a <span style="color: purple;">probability density function (PDF)</span>, whereas a discrete has a <span style="color: purple;">probability mass function (PMF)</span>.
:::

#### Example of a Discrete and Categorical Random Variable

. . .

$$Y = \text{Item obtained from the box.}$$

:::{style="font-size: 20px;"}
|Item | $Y$ | Probability|
|:---:|:-------:|:----------:|
| ![](images/banana.png){height="40"} | Banana  |     0.12|
| ![](images/bobomb.png){height="40"} | Bob-omb |     0.05|
| ![](images/coin.png){height="40"}   | Coin    |     0.75|
| ![](images/horn.png){height="40"}   | Horn    |     0.03|
| ![](images/shell.png){height="40"}  | Shell   |     0.05|

> **Attribution:** Images from [pngkey](https://www.pngkey.com/detail/u2w7e6o0i1q8i1y3_randome-clipart-mario-kart-mario-kart-8-deluxe/).
:::

#### Example of a Discrete and Count Random Variable

. . .

$$C = \text{Length of ship stay in days.}$$

| $C$ | Probability |
|:---:|:------:|
| 1 | 0.25 |
| 2 | 0.50 |
| 3 | 0.15 |
| 4 | 0.10 |

## 3. Measures of Central Tendency and Uncertainty

::: incremental
- These measures summarize the information of a probability distribution.
- They are subset as:
  + <span style="color: purple;">Central tendency:</span> a "typical" value in a random variable.
  + <span style="color: purple;">Uncertainty:</span> a measure of how "spread" the random variable is.
:::


### 3.1. Mode and Entropy in Discrete Random Variables

::: incremental
- Both measures apply to all classes of discrete random variables.
- The <span style="color: purple;">mode</span> is a measure of central tendency. It is the outcome having the highest probability.
:::

#### The Entropy

- It is a measure of uncertainty defined as

$$H(Y) = -\displaystyle \sum_y P(Y = y)\log[P(Y = y)].$$

::: incremental
- It is a nonnegative measure of uncertainty.
- <span style="color: purple;"> If its value is equal to zero, then there is no randomness. </span>
:::

#### Example

- What is the mode for $Y = \text{Item obtained from the box}$?

:::{style="font-size: 22px;"}
|Item | $Y$ | Probability|
|:---:|:-------:|:----------:|
| ![](images/banana.png){height="40"} | Banana  |     0.12|
| ![](images/bobomb.png){height="40"} | Bob-omb |     0.05|
| ![](images/coin.png){height="40"}   | Coin    |     0.75|
| ![](images/horn.png){height="40"}   | Horn    |     0.03|
| ![](images/shell.png){height="40"}  | Shell   |     0.05|

> **Attribution:** Images from [pngkey](https://www.pngkey.com/detail/u2w7e6o0i1q8i1y3_randome-clipart-mario-kart-mario-kart-8-deluxe/).
:::

#### How About the Entropy?

. . .

<br>

\begin{align*}
H(Y) &= -\displaystyle \sum_y P(Y = y)\log[P(Y = y)] \\
&= -[0.12 \log(0.12) + 0.05 \log(0.05) + \\
& \qquad \quad 0.75 \log(0.75) + 0.03 \log(0.03) + 0.05 \log(0.05)] \\
&= 0.87
\end{align*}

### 3.2. Mean and Variance

. . .

<br>

- Both measures apply to both discrete and continuous random variables (as long as they are <span style="color: purple;">numeric</span>!).

#### The Mean

- It is a measure of central tendency.

. . .

- If $X$ is discrete, with $P(X = x)$ as a PMF, then
$$\mathbb{E}(X) = \displaystyle \sum_x x \cdot P(X = x).$$
- If $X$ is continuous, with $f_X(x)$ as a PDF, then 
$$\mathbb{E}(X) = \displaystyle \int_x x \cdot f_X(x)  \text{d}x.$$

#### The Variance

<br>

- It is a measure of uncertainty.

. . .

$$\text{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}\{[X - \mathbb{E}(X)]^2\} = \mathbb{E}(X^2) - [\mathbb{E}(X)]^2.$$

- Note it is an expectation (specifically, <span style="color: purple;">the squared deviation from the mean</span>).
